title: Server rendering for a company site
metaTitle: Send the first view as HTML
excerpt: The first view of a marketing page should arrive as HTML, with the company already explained. A page that waits on the browser to do that is slower than it needs to be.
alt: A wide mountain valley with snowy peaks, a braided river, and evergreen trees in the foreground. The full view fits a piece about sending the whole first screen as HTML.
caption: The first response should already contain the view. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should be in the HTML of a marketing page?
faqs.answer: The company name, the headline, the supporting sentence, the primary action, and the navigation. View the source and read them there. Images that dominate the first screen should be in the document too, with dimensions and alt text, so the layout has a box before scripts run.

faqs.question: Does server rendering mean no JavaScript?
faqs.answer: No. Menus, dialogs, and extra form checks can run in the browser, and the explanation of the company should not depend on them. Disable JavaScript and reload. If the page is an empty shell, the script was doing the server's job.

faqs.question: How does this relate to loading speed?
faqs.answer: Google's Core Web Vitals guidance asks for largest contentful paint within 2.5 seconds. On a homepage that element is usually the headline or the hero image. If it is not in the first HTML, the wait includes downloading and running JavaScript. Sending it in the document removes that wait, though you still have to keep the image itself from being enormous.

sources.title: Understanding Core Web Vitals and Google search results

markdown:
A server rendered marketing site sends the first view as HTML. The headline, the offer, and the way to talk to you are in that document when it arrives. A page that waits on the browser to explain the company is slower than it needs to be, and it is blank for anyone whose script has not run yet.

The server's job is the page. The browser's job is the extra behavior: a menu, a form check, a small interaction. If you reverse those jobs, the company is trapped behind a download.

## What "the first view" has to contain

Open the page and view the source, before you admire the result in the browser. You should be able to read the company name, the headline, the supporting sentence, the primary action, and the navigation. Those strings are HTML, not strings waiting inside a JavaScript bundle.

Images that carry the first impression can be in the HTML too, with their dimensions and their alt text, so the layout has a box and the words around it are not the only content. A hero that exists only after a component mounts will pop in late, and the late pop is the page shifting under the reader.

Google's [Core Web Vitals](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/core-web-vitals) set the loading target: largest contentful paint within 2.5 seconds. On a company homepage the largest element is usually the headline or the hero photograph. If that element is not in the first HTML, the clock includes the script download, the parse, and the render, on the visitor's phone, on the visitor's network. Sending the element in the document removes that wait from the critical path. You can still miss 2.5 seconds with a huge image. You will miss it more reliably if you also wait for JavaScript to decide what the image is.

Client-side rendering can be the right tool for a signed-in product that has no public content. A marketing site is public content. Treat it that way. A redesign is the moment this rule gets lost. The new page looks richer in a prototype, the prototype is a client app, and the launch ships the prototype. Keep the prototype as a picture of the hierarchy. Rebuild the first view as HTML. The animation, if you still want it, can start after the words are already readable. A visitor on a train should not have to wait for your bundle to learn the name of the company.

## What can wait for the browser

The menu button can enhance a list that is already in the document. A dialog can open with script. A form can check an email format before the submit, as long as the server checks it again. A carousel can be script, or it can be a list that does not need a carousel.

What should not wait is the explanation. If the script fails, is blocked, or is slow, the company is still legible. Disable JavaScript in the browser and reload. You should still know who you are looking at and what to do next. If you see an empty shell, the page was an application pretending to be a site.

Third-party tags are the usual way this goes wrong after a careful build. A chat widget, an experiment tool, and an analytics snippet race the headline. Load them after the page has painted, or do not load them on the first view. A tag that injects a banner above the hero will also push the layout down. Reserve space or refuse the banner. Layout shift has its own target in the same Core Web Vitals guidance: a cumulative layout shift under 0.1. A late banner is a direct hit on that number, and it is a direct hit on the headline you wanted read.

Authentication walls do not belong on the marketing pages. The portal can be a client application. The public story should not be. Keep that split clean so a campaign URL never depends on a session to say what the company does.

## How a Next.js site does this without a second stack

Next.js can render a page to HTML on the server and send that document first. On a Hanabi site that is the default posture for the marketing pages: React components that produce HTML, styled with Tailwind, deployed on Vercel. The interactive pieces stay small. A page does not need to become a client component because it has a link in it.

Use the server render for anything a stranger should read. Fetch the published words on the server, from the CMS or from the repository, and include them in the response. A loading spinner where the headline should be is a choice to wait. Spinners are for actions a person just took, not for the company's name.

Static generation is a good fit when the page changes when you publish, not on every request. The HTML can be ready before the visit. Dynamic rendering is a good fit when the page depends on the request and still needs to be complete in the response. Either way, the visitor receives HTML. The failure mode is a shell that says it will fill in later. Later is the delay you are trying to remove.

Hydration is the step where React attaches to that HTML so clicks work. The text should not change during hydration. If the server HTML says one headline and the client replaces it, you will see a flicker, and you may shift the layout. Make the two outputs match. A timestamp, a random testimonial, or a theme that is only known on the client are the usual mismatches. Decide them on the server, or reserve their space so the swap does not move the page.

## The test that keeps the rule honest

Run it on a phone, on a slow connection, and with the cache cleared. The test is not a perfect score in a lab. The test is whether the company is readable early.

- View source contains the headline and the primary action.
- With JavaScript disabled, those are still visible.
- The largest element does not wait on a bundle to exist.
- No banner inserts itself above the hero after load.
- Hydration does not swap the words.
- The main navigation is real links.

Do this again after you add a tool. New tools like to own the first paint. Most of them do not need to. If a vendor's install snippet replaces your document with their loader, the vendor is a bad fit for a marketing page, however useful the widget is inside a signed-in product.

Watch the hero image's weight in the same pass. Server HTML that references a four-megabyte photograph has moved the wait from the script to the file. The rendering model did its job. The image still needs a crop and a modern format. Those are separate decisions, and they matter because the image is often what the loading metric is timing.

## What this changes for the writer

The people editing the site should be editing content that drops into the template, not editing a canvas that only exists in the browser. A heading in the CMS becomes a heading in the HTML. A missing field becomes a missing sentence you can see in the source, not a blank box that appears after a spinner.

Preview has to show that same HTML, in the same template, before the page is public. A preview that is an admin form will not catch a headline that breaks the layout or a hero that never arrives. The public template is the preview. The draft flag is what keeps it unpublished.

This also keeps the page shareable. When someone pastes the URL into a chat, the title and the description have a document to come from. You still write those fields on purpose. The server render is what makes them belong to the same page the visitor gets, rather than to a shell that hopes the script will catch up.

## A boundary worth keeping

Not every screen on the domain should be a static document. The client portal, the CMS admin, and a signed-in tool can be applications. They have empty states, permissions, and data that should not be in a public cache. The marketing site is the opposite: public, stable, and complete in the first response.

Cache the public HTML at the edge when the page does not depend on the visitor. A company story that is the same for everyone should not be rebuilt in the browser, and it often should not be rebuilt on every request. Invalidate that cache when you publish, so the fresh headline arrives as HTML too. If a page is both, split it. The story is HTML. The tool behind a link can be the application. A homepage that is half story and half live dashboard will be as slow as the dashboard and as vague as a tool that has not loaded. Give the story the server render. Give the tool its own route.

Forms are the next place a marketing page quietly turns into a pile of scripts. [Forms that post without a maze of scripts](/blog/forms-that-post-without-a-maze-of-scripts) is the next piece. A form needs a place to land, a confirmation, and a way to see failures. A widget you cannot debug on launch day is a risk the server-rendered page should not take.

The result of this approach is visible in the work itself. See [selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works) for sites that can explain the company without asking the browser to assemble it first.
